Principal Component Analysis · Too many features03

A new set of axes

Principal Component Analysis (PCA) is an   algorithm.

It finds us a   for our data, chosen so that:

  • Most of the variance in the dataset lies along the first few axes.
  • The axes are orthogonal to each other, so the new features are uncorrelated.

PCA is just a  .

Principal Component Analysis · Too many features04

The road ahead

PCA is five steps.

  1. Standardize the datapage 10Zero mean and unit variance for every feature.
  2. Covariance matrixpage 12How much every pair of features moves together.
  3. Eigenvalues and eigenvectorspp. 13–16The new axes, and the variance along each.
  4. Sort thempage 17Largest variance first.
  5. Choose how many to keeppp. 18–26Drop the axes that barely matter.

Principal Component Analysis · Too many features05

Variance

A dataset is only interesting if its samples are different from each other.

We measure how spread out a feature is with its  .

\text{Var}(x) = \frac{1}{n-1}\sum_i (x_i - \mu)^2

Typically, the higher the variance of a feature, the more   it can give us about the data.

Principal Component Analysis · Variance and covariance06

Covariance

Features in our dataset often have some relationship to each other, like height and weight. We measure that with the   between two features a and b:

\text{Cov}(a, b) = \frac{1}{n-1}\sum_i (a_i - \mu_a)(b_i - \mu_b)

The more two features overlap ( ), the more overlapping information they carry.

Quick check: what is the covariance of a feature with itself?
Principal Component Analysis · Variance and covariance07

The covariance matrix

We collect them all in one d by d table, the   C.

C = \Hb{\begin{matrix} \text{Var}(a) & \text{Cov}(a,b) \\ \text{Cov}(a,b) & \text{Var}(b) \end{matrix}}
  • The diagonal holds each feature's variance.
  • Everything off the diagonal is a covariance, and the matrix is symmetric.
C = \frac{1}{n-1}\,X\T X

PCA's goal in one sentence: find new axes where this matrix has   everywhere off the diagonal.

2. The covariance matrix

From the covariance matrix we can read the relationships between our features:

  • Covariance > 0: features change together.
  • Covariance < 0: features change opposite of each other.
  • Covariance ≈ 0: features mostly don't have a relationship.

Ours is 0.76:  , just like the picture.

Principal Component Analysis · PCA by hand12

What are we looking for?

A direction is a row v of length 1.

z = x\,v\T

The first new axis is the direction with the  .

\text{Var}(z) = v\,C\,v\T
Principal Component Analysis · PCA by hand13

Why eigenvectors?

C\,v\T = \lambda\,v\T

Directions like that are called   of C, and their stretch factors λ are  .

  • The   are the directions our new axes point.
  • The   are the variance along each of them.
Principal Component Analysis · PCA by hand14

3. Eigenvalues

A nonzero v can only be squashed to zero if the matrix C − λI has a  .

\det(C - \lambda I) = 0 \text{our}\ C\text{, with}\ \lambda\ \text{subtracted on the diagonal} \det\Hb{\begin{matrix} 1-\lambda & 0.76 \\ 0.76 & 1-\lambda \end{matrix}} = 0 2 \times 2\ \text{determinant: } ad - bc (1-\lambda)^2 - 0.76^2 = 0 \text{square root of both sides} 1 - \lambda = \pm 0.76

Two answers, one for each new axis:

3. Eigenvectors

Now we find the direction that goes with each eigenvalue.

\Hb{\begin{matrix} -0.76 & 0.76 \\ 0.76 & -0.76 \end{matrix}} \Hb{\begin{matrix} a \\ b \end{matrix}} = \Hb{\begin{matrix} 0 \\ 0 \end{matrix}} \text{both rows say the same thing} a = b \text{scale to length 1} v_1 = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[1,\ 1] \approx [0.71,\ 0.71]

Doing the same for λ2 = 0.24 gives a = −b, so  .

4. Sort them

We sort the eigenvalues from largest to smallest, and their eigenvectors along with them. The sorted directions are the  :

Going back

Almost: walk z steps along the direction we kept.

\hat{x} = z\,v
  • What we lose is the variance on the dropped components. Here that's λ2 = 0.24, the missing  .
  • Back to real units: undo step 1 by multiplying by σ and adding μ. Student 1 comes back as about 10.8 in math and 5.7 in physics. They really scored 10 and 6.
\hat{x} = z_1 v_1 + z_2 v_2 + \dots + z_k v_k
Principal Component Analysis · PCA by hand20

That won't scale

Finding the roots of a big polynomial is  .

We instead use something called the   (SVD), which works on the data directly:

X = U\,\Sigma\,V\T

Remember, PCA is just trying to find a new set of axes for the data, and a change of axes is a  .

Principal Component Analysis · The shortcut: SVD21

Rotate, stretch, rotate

Any linear transformation can be described as a  , then a   along the axes, then another  .

  • VT rotates. Its rows are perpendicular directions of length 1.
  • Σ stretches. It's zero except on its diagonal, which holds the singular values σ1 ≥ σ2 ≥ …, already sorted.
  • U rotates again.
Principal Component Analysis · The shortcut: SVD22

The SVD hands us PCA

Because U is a rotation, UT U = I and it cancels:

C = \frac{1}{n-1}\,X\T X = \frac{1}{n-1}\,V\,\Sigma\,U\T\,U\,\Sigma\,V\T U\T U = I C = V\,\frac{\Sigma^2}{n-1}\,V\T
  •   are the eigenvectors: our principal components.
  •   holds the eigenvalues, after squaring and dividing by n − 1:
\lambda_k = \frac{\sigma_k^2}{n-1}

Steps 2, 3 and 4 all come out of one decomposition, and we never build C at all.

Principal Component Analysis · The shortcut: SVD23

PCA in numpy

Here's our whole worked example. Standardize, then one call to the SVD:

import numpy as np
# math and physics scores for six students
X = np.array([[10, 6], [11, 4], [8, 5],
[3, 3], [1, 3.2], [2, 1]])
# step 1: standardize each column
Z = (X - X.mean(axis=0)) / X.std(axis=0, ddof=1)
# steps 2 to 4 in one call
U, S, Vt = np.linalg.svd(Z, full_matrices=False)
print(Vt.round(3)) # directions
print(S.round(2)) # singular values
print((S**2 / (len(X) - 1)).round(3)) # variances
# step 5: keep only PC 1
z = Z @ Vt[0]
print(z.round(2))

How many should we keep?

For our digits,   components keep 90% of the variance and   keep 95%.

Principal Component Analysis · Using PCA26

Does the model mind?

With just   of the 64 components we match the accuracy of using every pixel. Fewer dimensions means:

  • Faster training and prediction, and less to store.
  • Denser data, so "nearby" means something again.
  • Less noise. The components we drop are often mostly noise, so some models even improve.

PCA in Python

In practice we use scikit-learn's PCA, which centers the data and runs the SVD for us:

from sklearn.datasets import load_digits
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier
X, y = load_digits(return_X_y=True) # 64 pixels per image
X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(
X, y, test_size=0.3, random_state=0, stratify=y)
# learn the new axes from the training data only
pca = PCA(n_components=16).fit(X_tr)
Z_tr, Z_te = pca.transform(X_tr), pca.transform(X_te)
print(Z_tr.shape)
print(round(pca.explained_variance_ratio_.sum(), 3))
knn = KNeighborsClassifier(5).fit(Z_tr, y_tr)
print(round(knn.score(Z_te, y_te), 3))
Output

Principal Component Analysis · Using PCA29

Where PCA misleads

PCA is unsupervised: it keeps the directions with the most variance, and the most variance isn't always the  .

  • It's linear. PCA can rotate, but it can't unbend. Curved structure needs something like the kernels of Chapter 4.
  • It's scale sensitive. Measure a feature in different units and you get different components. Standardize first.
  • It's harder to explain. "Component 3" is a mixture of every feature, not something you can point to.
  • It's swayed by outliers. One extreme point can pull a whole component toward itself.
  • It can leak. Fit PCA on the training data only, then apply those same axes to validation and test data.
Principal Component Analysis · Using PCA30

Cheat sheet

The whole algorithm

  1. Standardize: subtract each feature's average, divide by its standard deviation.
  2. Covariance matrix C.
  3. Eigenvectors and eigenvalues of C.
  4. Sort by eigenvalue, largest first.
  5. Keep the first k and project.
C = \frac{1}{n-1}\,X\T X C\,v\T = \lambda\,v\T z = x\,v\T \qquad \hat{x} = z\,v \frac{\lambda_k}{\lambda_1 + \lambda_2 + \dots + \lambda_d} X = U\,\Sigma\,V\T,\qquad \lambda_k = \frac{\sigma_k^2}{n-1}

Remember

  • Eigenvectors are directions; eigenvalues are variance.
  • The components are orthogonal, so the new features are uncorrelated.
  • Rotating never changes the total variance.
  • PCA is unsupervised and linear. Scale first; fit on training data only.
Principal Component Analysis · Using PCA31

Practice problems

  1. Variance by hand. A feature has the values 2, 4 and 6. What are its average, variance and standard deviation?
  2. Reading a matrix. Two features have variances 4 and 9, and covariance −3. Write their covariance matrix. Do they move together or opposite?
  3. Two components. Two standardized features have a covariance of 0.5. Find both eigenvalues and the share of the variance on PC 1.
  4. Projecting. A standardized point is x = [2, 1] and PC 1 is v = [0.6, 0.8]. Is v a valid direction? Where does x land on it?
  5. How many? A dataset's eigenvalues are 5, 3, 1.5 and 0.5. How much variance do the first two components keep? How many do we need for 95%?
  6. From the SVD. A centered dataset with 10 points has singular values 6 and 2. What are the eigenvalues of its covariance matrix?
  7. Going back. In problem 4 we kept only z. Rebuild the point from it. How far is the rebuilt point from the real x = [2, 1]?
  8. Units. We run PCA on income (in dollars) and age (in years) without standardizing. What will PC 1 look like, and why?
  9. Reading a scree plot. The eigenvalues are 4.0, 3.5, 0.3, 0.1 and 0.1. Where is the elbow? How many would you keep?
  10. Spot the leak. A classmate fits PCA on the whole dataset, then splits it into training and test sets. What went wrong?
